newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FOCUS - Portuguese stocks surge on economy hopes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Portuguese stocks surge on economy hopes.

text.p: Portuguese share prices surged to record highs on Monday, driven up by stock-hungry investment funds and optimism about the country's economy.
But some traders warned that Monday's advance, which took gains since the start of the year to three percent, may have been overdone and that a correction was probably imminent.

"Today's rise seems to me to be exaggerated," said one trader who asked not to be named. "(But) there are many investment funds, mainly domestic, which have a lot of money and are buying with force," he added.
Lisbon's PSI20 index, which covers 20 leading blue chips, rose 2.24 percent to 5,317.31 points, just a shade below the 5,318.76 point peak hit earlier in the session.
Leading the pack, in terms of volume, was state-controlled Portugal Telecom which soared some 4.7 percent to 4,675 escudos ($29.8) per share in heavy trade of nearly 600,000 stocks.

Some analysts have said that the telecom stock, the most liquid on the Portuguese market, could target 5,000 escudos in the short term because investors still see it as cheap compared with other European telecommunications shares.
But the buying spread across the board, with insurer Mundial Confianca leaping 7.5 percent and wood group Sonae Industria gaining just over six percent.

Traders said that apart from Portugal Telecom, for which there was strong foreign interest, the motor for the price gains came from domestic funds which have apparently decided to boost their weightings in Portuguese stocks.

Portuguese investment funds traditionally keep a low proportion of their assets in stocks, but falling interest rates and the good outlook for the local economy have persuaded them to look more closely at the bourse, analysts said.
Despite the fact that the Lisbon stock market was one of the best performers in Europe last year, gaining over 30 percent, analysts believe that the bull run is far from exhausted.
According to a recent Reuter survey, analysts see the market index gaining a further 15 to 20 percent in 1997.

Investor appetite will be wetted by a series of privatisations, including the profitable EDP state electricity company, and the prospect of corporate profits being boosted by lower interest rates and faster economic growth than elsewhere in Europe.
